title: What AI skills or repos you are using when developing games?
author: Colonel-James-Parker
selftext:
I'm a Project/Product Manager. So even though I can't write codes myself, I kind of have technical background.   
  
In past 5 months I'm creating some projects with the help of AI. Started with Claude, but last 2 months using Codex Pro. Released a simple app on IOS a month ago to experience the whole vibe coding process.  
  
Even did a 2D platformer/puzzle type of browser game for my girlfriend as birthday gift. But now, I'm thinking of making a real but not very complicated game. 

So I wanted to ask you experienced guys, which skills or github repos should I look into for Codex when game developing? 

I understand it may differ based on engine or structure, but maybe you would tell me some general advices. Thanks in advance.

comments.author: teamharder
comments.body: What engine? I'm working with Unity. I've built up a pretty sizable skill with a good amount of tools connected to that skill. It's mainly just a thin orchestrator with about 20 different sub-agent workers that have different specializations. Last night I had it build a .exe museum of prefab assets that I've been collecting while on sale, so I could go shopping for village, city, and environmental assets for the RPG game I'm working on.

replies.author: Colonel-James-Parker
replies.body:
I never experienced with any of engines. I've downloaded Godot and Unity, tried them a bit only. 

My game would be a mix of tycoon, career sim and idle-game. Even I want to do some 3D office rooms and characters but I'm not sure if I can learn Unity or put valuable enough time for that. Of course if that requires, I have to do it.

replies.author: teamharder
replies.body:
Lol you don't have to learn anything now. It'd help some, but it's not necessary. I know how to pull in assets off of the asset store and download them and how to connect the MCP server and that's about it. Claude has done literally everything else.


Instead of learning how to use Unity, I've been spending that time evolving the skills to be able to be accurate and efficient with Unity. Also spending time looking over other professional polished games or listening to other developers speak is also valuable because then you can at least ask for and know what to look for when creating a game.


Maybe I'm wrong about it being necessary or not but it's worked so far for me.

replies.author: Colonel-James-Parker
replies.body: Thank you so much. I'll definitely look into this from this angle and check them out.

replies.author: teamharder
replies.body: Also check out the current Unity sale running. 90-98% off a bunch off assets packs. https://assetstore.unity.com/?price=0-4&on_sale=true&orderBy=1&rows=96

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
Yea, I'm focusing myself on understanding the philosophy of making a game.  What makes A fun while B falls flat?  When is something compelling and when is something boring or trite.  

I'm worried about the artistic vision of my game, but AI does great art.  But I think I'd rather find a human who can come up with something distinct.  I dont see pictures in my head, so it's hard for me to describe the way I want my game to look.  Plus, working with humans is more fun that working alone.  + ai.  

I'm having issues with bug hunting.  Not in the code, when the rare issue arrives, we fix it easily, and it's always been that the AI and I just think that part through clearly enough.  An oversight.  But when the bug is on the engine side, the AI tends to take the most common, easy path, the path of training.  It has me check stuff thats the equivalent of checking if your device is plugged in.  I think it's because it can't see the project, just the pattern of our chat window.  So if cant see when what it thinks is true (thinks is doing a lot of work here), and the ground truth.

replies.author: teamharder
replies.body: That's been a huge chunk of my Claude skill. Tools to check things quickly meaning fewer tokens burned. Screenshots paired with cheap sub agents to verify. Many many many lessons learned.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
I've heard of the hierarchical network of AI (agents?) that people use to work on projects, with specific roles, and it seems like a great idea.  Context drift and contamination is bad.  But it also seems expensive.  Is it?  Should I look into seeing it if will work well for my project?  

For context, I cant afford the 200 plan.

replies.author: teamharder
replies.body:
In my experience it's more efficient with rate limits. The skill is basically a thin document that tells the CEO (router) "if I'm asking about X kind of task, go hire the appropriate employee and point him at the appropriate documentation". E.g. I type /game-dev and I tell Opus to add VFX to my characters skill > he wakes up, reads the skill, sees Vfx tasks should go to the VFX sub-agent > Opus spools up a cheaper sub-agent and says "here's the task, go read this .MD to know how to do your job" > Opus doesn't read the "employee manual" for that job, he just says "there's the bookshelf, go read it" > employee reads the hand off from CEO and the manual, does the work and reports back to the CEO > CEO verifies the work and reports to me. 


The question is "why not just have the smart CEO do everything? Delegation like that seems overly complex and cumbersome". Sure, the CEO burns tokens handing out jobs and I use more tokens overall. BUT those tokens are distributed across many agents. I use Opus 1 million token context models and I never go above 400-500k tokens with that one window, even in a 4-6 hour overnight session. Each sub agent burns 50-200k tokens, but that never clutters the main window or each other. These models become more expensive and dumb as you get closer to their token limit.


Also, the employee gets a clean and simple task every time. No extra crap to distract him. If he does a really bad job? Instead of working further with a bad employee, the CEO fires him and hires another. If models make a mistake once, they're likely to make it again. 


Overlord? Nah. They're smarter than I am. The only thing I've got on them is taste and a set of eyeballs. Business owner with employees is more how it feels.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
That game sounds like it comes from lived experience. Good idea.  

You don't have to learn any of these engines.  It'll make things faster if your comfortable with them, but that will come.  AI knows how to build what you want.  You just have to be very good about conveying that idea to it.  It will pattern match whatever you describe.  And I doubt you can ever perfectly convey your idea, so be ready to course correct.

I would also suggest you learn the... philosophy of coding.  You don't need to know how to write perfect code, but if you can follow the logic, you can spot where it drifts from your vision.  Also, you can always ask AI to explain what it's writing.  Also, tell it to ask you for direction for any part it's not sure it understands.  If the prediction isn't certain, it'll mostly ask you.

comments.author: pennystudio
comments.body: I only started 2 months ago, but the game I am building is more elaborate. At the beginning of the project I found that gstack (from Garry Tan's repo) is very useful, it can help you focus, plan architecture, push out a MVP fast instead of keep refining. But as the project progressed, Claude seems to learn and I seem to be getting better at instructing, I found myself rarely use it now.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
I started my current project by spending days trying to crystalize/clarify the idea of the game I wanted.  Seems the better I can convey the idea, the better it can pattern match/predict/ build it.  Every issue so far has been when my concept was vague in certain areas or I wasnt clear enough.  Or I hadnt decided yet.  I just had to spend a couple days working on the design side with AI to take the idea to the next level of clarity.  I wonder how many more times I'll have to do that.  

But damn is opus smart.

comments.author: Bratchan
comments.body: Scope you should know this.  Planning out your game first will help you the most. make a game design document..  from there decide is it simple enough to that it might be able to be made with  html/js or maybe even phaser..  or do you need something with a bit more power like godot/unity

replies.author: Colonel-James-Parker
replies.body:
Yeah, I'm starting every project with documents first before even starting a single line of design or code. 

I did my first 2d platformer game with phaser, it was fun. Now I'm thinking of making somethings 2.5D or 3D. Even using Meshy for some content generation but in the end, I guess I need to learn a little bit of engines.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: The tools of asset generation are growing all the time.  Every time I look, I'm like holy cow, theres a tool for that now?  amazing.

comments.author: Just-Limit9072
comments.body: phraser is your friend for 2d browsers
